name: Opening traps
goal: You can spot common opening traps, such as attacks on f2 and f7, and avoid falling into them.
intro: An opening trap is a position where a natural-looking move loses at once. Most traps catch a player who grabs material, or develops a piece, without asking what the opponent can do next. In this Lesson you spring two famous traps and step around two others. The habit to keep: before each move, ask what your opponent's last move threatens, and what your own move leaves undefended.

parts.title: A pin that does not hold
parts.keyIdea: A piece pinned to the queen may still move when losing the queen leads to mate, or when the pinning piece is left undefended.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Philidor Defence. You are White. Black's bishop on g4 pins your f3 knight to your queen, and Black has just spent a move on ...h6 instead of developing. Is your knight really stuck?

notes.text: 5.Nxe5 takes a pawn and leaves your queen to be taken. If Black takes back with 5...dxe5, your queen now sees the bishop on g4, and 6.Qxg4 leaves you a pawn up. If Black grabs your queen, a mate follows.
Black took the queen with 5...Bxd1, the losing choice. 6.Bxf7+ leaves the king one legal move, to e7: the knight on e5 protects your bishop, and it also covers d7.

7.Nd5# is Legal's Mate. The d5 knight gives check and covers f6, the bishop on f7 covers e6 and e8, the e5 knight covers d7 and guards the bishop, and Black's own queen, pawn and bishop block d8, d6 and f8. Two knights and a bishop have beaten a whole extra queen.

parts.title: Legal's Mate in reverse, on f2
parts.keyIdea: Before you pin a piece to the queen, ask whether your opponent could ignore the pin and mate you on f2.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Stafford Gambit. You are White and a pawn up, but Black's bishop on c5 already aims at f2, the weak square next to your king. In the game White pinned the f6 knight with 6.Bg5 and was mated three moves later. Find a safer developing move.

notes.text: 6.Be2 develops, gets you ready to castle and covers g4, a square Black's pieces want for an attack on f2. The tempting 6.Bg5, pinning the knight, would lose to Legal's Mate turned around: 6...Nxe4 7.Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8.Ke2 Bg4#, and other replies to 6...Nxe4 lose a lot of material.
Black's knight jumped to g4 anyway, aiming at f2 together with the bishop. 7.Bxg4 removes it. Black wins the piece back with 7...Qh4, which attacks your bishop and f2 at the same time.
8.g3 attacks the queen and blocks its path to f2. After 8...Qxg4 9.Qxg4 Bxg4 the queens come off, f2 is safe, and you are still a pawn up.

parts.title: A knight takes on d5
parts.keyIdea: When a piece leaves a square, look at the lines it opens: a check along a newly opened line can win back more than you give.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Queen's Gambit Declined: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5. You are Black. White's knight has just left c3 to take your pawn on d5. Look at the squares between your bishop on f8 and White's king on e1, and count what each side could take.
parts.line: Nxd5 Bxd8 Bb4+ Qd2 Bxd2+ Kxd2 Kxd8

notes.text: 6...Nxd5 takes the knight. Your queen on d8 is now open to the bishop on g5, but with White's knight gone from c3, your bishop on f8 can reach b4 and check White's king along the diagonal from b4 to e1.
White took your queen with 7.Bxd8. 7...Bb4+ checks along that open diagonal. White's king has no square to go to, so White's only legal move is 8.Qd2, putting the queen in the way.
8...Bxd2+ takes the queen, again with check, and White's king has to take back.

9...Kxd8 takes the bishop on d8. Now count: White has taken a pawn, your queen and a bishop; you have taken a knight, the queen and a bishop. You are a knight up for a pawn, thanks to the diagonal White's knight opened when it left c3.

parts.title: Mind the pin on the e-file
parts.keyIdea: When a pawn in front of your king is pinned, it cannot take a checking piece: keep a square empty for the king.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Caro-Kann Defence. You are Black. White has just played the odd-looking 5.Qe2, putting the queen on the e-file with your king, and White's knight on e4 between them. In the game Black developed in the most natural way and was mated on the next move. Find a safe developing move.

notes.text: 5...Ndf6 moves the d7 knight to f6, where it challenges the e4 knight, and d7 stays empty for your king. The natural 5...Ngf6 would lose to 6.Nd6#, a smothered mate: the e7 pawn cannot take the knight because the queen on e2 pins it to your king, and your own pieces fill every square around the king. 5...Qc7, which covers d6, is also safe.
After 6.Nf3, 6...Nxe4 trades knights. White's queen has to take back, and it stands in the open where your pieces can attack it.
7...Nf6 develops with a threat to the queen on e4, so White must spend another move on it. You have side-stepped the trap and kept a sound position.
